Good morning.
My name is Martin Maxa, from the Department of Measurement here at this faculty.
I worked on this together with Jakub Svatoš, from the same department.
Today I will talk about acoustic detection, classification and localization of impulsive sounds, with gunshots as the target class.
The main focus is gunshot classification: we compare different cepstral features and two classifiers.
I will also briefly show the localization.

Slide 2 – Motivation and research questions [0:45–1:50]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
This work is part of the development of an acoustic sensor system for the protection of soft targets.
Acoustic detection can complement camera-based surveillance.
Sound is omnidirectional, and it does not need a direct line of sight.
[CUT] The complete system should detect an impulsive event, classify it, ideally down to the calibre, and localize its source.
It should also work outdoors, where there is noise and many reflections. [/CUT]
[CLICK]
We focus on three questions.
First, which cepstral representation works best for separating gunshots from similar impulsive sounds?
Second, which classifier performs better: a neural network or a support vector machine?
And third, how does the frame length affect the results?

Slide 3 – The acoustic signature of a gunshot [1:50–3:00]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
Let us first look at the signal of a gunshot.
A gunshot has one or two components, depending on the projectile speed.
A subsonic shot has only the muzzle blast; a supersonic projectile also produces a shock wave.
This recording is a supersonic shot, so we see both.
The first component, at about two and a half milliseconds, is the shock wave.
[CUT] It is produced along the projectile trajectory and has a characteristic N-shaped pressure profile. [/CUT]
[CLICK]
The second one, about forty-five milliseconds later, is the muzzle blast.
It comes from the gases at the barrel and is present in every gunshot.
Between and after these two components, we mainly see reflections from the surroundings.
They matter for the choice of frame length, and I will return to them in the results.

Slide 4 – Single-domain analysis is insufficient [3:00–3:30]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
This also shows why one signal domain alone is not enough.
The spectrum often describes the environment more than the gunshot itself.
The time-domain shape changes during propagation and because of obstacles.
So we need features that combine both domains, and cepstral features do exactly that.

Slide 5 – Proposed system architecture [3:30–4:20]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
Now let us look at the proposed system.
It consists of several independent sensor units connected to a remote server.
Each sensor continuously monitors its surroundings.
When it detects an impulsive event, it sends the recorded signal to the server.
The server then performs two main tasks: classification of the event and localization of the sound source.
Several units give wider coverage and allow us to estimate the source position.
The system was tested with several firearm calibres and ammunition types.

Slide 6 – Localization – bearing from TDoA [4:20–5:20]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
First, I will briefly explain the localization.
Each sensor unit has two MEMS microphones, about twenty centimetres apart, sampled at 44.1 kilohertz.
We measure the time difference of arrival between the two microphones.
From this delay, we can calculate the direction to the source using the equation shown here.
[CLICK]
One sensor unit therefore gives us one direction.
With two sensor units, we get two directions, and their intersection gives us the estimated source position.
We tested this on seventy events at nine reference angles.
Using cross-correlation with parabolic interpolation, we achieved a mean absolute error of zero point seven seven degrees.

Slide 7 – Feature extraction – cepstral coefficients [5:20–5:50]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
Now I will move to the main part of the work: classification.
We compared four different cepstral feature extractors.
All of them use the same chain: framing, FFT, a filter bank, and then a logarithm and a discrete cosine transform.
The main difference is the filter bank.
You can see all four filter banks here, drawn on the same frequency axis.

Slide 8 – Feature extraction – the four filter banks [5:50–6:25]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
MFCC uses the mel scale, with dense filters at low frequencies.
It comes from speech processing, but it also works for gunshots.
LFCC uses linearly spaced filters, while IMFCC uses an inverted mel scale, with dense filters at high frequencies.
GTCC uses a gammatone filter bank based on a model of the human auditory system.
It is also reported to be more robust to noise than MFCC.

Slide 10 – Classification results – MCC at a glance [6:40–7:35]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
This chart shows the same results, but only the Matthews correlation coefficient.
MCC considers the whole confusion matrix, so it is less affected by class imbalance than accuracy.
The red line is GTCC.
It is on top in both panels and for every frame length.
The neural network gives better results than the SVM, and the difference grows with longer frames.
The best configuration is GTCC with the neural network and a fifty-millisecond frame.
It reaches an accuracy of ninety-nine point one five percent, a recall of ninety-six point seven seven percent, and an MCC of zero point nine eight.
That is one hundred and seventeen correct decisions out of one hundred and eighteen test events.

Slide 11 – Discussion [7:35–8:45]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
From these results, we can make three main observations.
First, MFCC, LFCC and IMFCC give similar results, so the filter spacing makes little difference.
Second, GTCC performs clearly better.
[CUT] One possible reason is that the gammatone filter bank is based on an auditory model and is known to be more robust to noise.
However, we did not study this mechanism directly. [/CUT]
Third, the neural network performs slightly better than the SVM, especially with longer frames.
This is a general trend, not true for every single result.
[CLICK]
Finally, longer frames generally improve the classification accuracy.
But with a fifty-millisecond frame, we already start to include more reflections from the environment, not only the gunshot itself.
So even longer frames would not necessarily help.

Slide 12 – Conclusion [8:45–9:30]
Say the whole slide.
column2:
To conclude.
We presented a distributed acoustic sensor system for the detection, classification and localization of impulsive sounds.
For gunshot classification, cepstral features work well with both tested classifiers.
Among the tested features, GTCC gives the best results.
The neural network also performs slightly better than the SVM, especially with longer frames.
The system was evaluated on real firearms with several calibres and ammunition types.
Thank you.
